summary:
Importance

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM.

Objective

To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM.

Design, setting, and participants

Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020).

Exposure

Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies).

Main outcomes and measures

Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM.

Results

Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%).

Conclusions and relevance

In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.
title: A Common CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy in Individuals of African Ancestry.

summary:
Importance

One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming.

Objective

To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support.

Design, setting, and participants

Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets.

Main outcomes and measures

A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system.

Results

Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system.

Conclusions and relevance

In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.
title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.

summary: Medicare Program; Implementation of Sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CMS-4214-P) Background On Oct. 16, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a proposed rule to implement key sections of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026 including section 6220 (Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act) and section 6224 (Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability). This rule also proposes a conforming change mandated by section 6219 of the CAA (Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals) that would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals. Implementing Certain Provisions of Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 On February 3, 2026, the CAA of 2026, which included several changes to the MA and Part D programs, was signed into law. In this rule, we are proposing to implement the following sections: Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals (Section 6219): This proposed rule implements Section 6219 of the CAA that would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals at or below 100% of the Federal Poverty Level, effective for plan years starting Jan. 1, 2028. Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act (Section 6220): CMS proposes to codify regulations to implement the REAL Health Providers Act, which establishes new provider directory verification and accuracy requirements for MA organizations beginning in contract year 2028. Specifically, CMS proposes requirements to implement this new law related to provider directory verification and maintenance standards, annual accuracy analysis and reporting, public reporting of accuracy scores, and cost-sharing protections for enrollees who rely on inaccurate provider directory information. CMS also proposes to codify the statutory requirements for contract year 2029, including that CMS must publicly display provider directory accuracy scores in a machine-readable format, and MA organizations must prominently display those scores in their provider directories. Through these proposed codifications implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS seeks to promote provider directory accuracy and accountability among MA organizations to ensure that beneficiaries are provided with clear, accurate information on the network of providers available to meet their healthcare needs. Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability (Section 6224): CMS has several proposals to implement section 6224 of the CAA, which established requirements related to pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and their affiliates specific to the Medicare Part D program. These proposals include new requirements governing the remuneration that PBMs and their affiliates may receive for services in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, data reporting by PBMs to Part D prescription drug plan (PDP) sponsors and CMS, transparency in PBM price guarantee arrangements, disclosure by PBMs to PDP sponsors of the terms of certain agreements between PBMs or their affiliates and pharmaceutical manufacturers, and other requirements added by the CAA. CMS also proposes to define key terms related to such requirements and establish compliance and enforcement mechanisms, including disgorgement of funds to CMS for violations of the remuneration requirements. The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. View this regulation on the Federal Register . The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary: Background: AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective: This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods: The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network–based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of –10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions: Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. For researchers, developers, and regulators, these findings highlight the need for standardized multimethod image-quality evaluation, complete reporting, and rigorous external validation before synthetic-image pipelines are translated into clinical AI applications. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD42023369125;
title: Quality Assessment and Model Training Impact of Synthetic Images in Medical Diagnostic Imaging: Systematic Review

summary:
Background

Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting.

Objective

To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines.

Design

Population-based U.S. cohort study.

Setting

Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases.

Participants

Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth.

Measurements

Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant.

Results

In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge.

Limitations

Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth.

Conclusion

No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.
title: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations.

summary:
Background

The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain.

Methods

In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90.

Results

The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group.

Conclusions

Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).
title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.

summary:
Background

The United States recently proposed changes to the recommendations for childhood hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination.

Objective

To project the effect of vaccine policy changes, if fully implemented, on chronic HBV infections.

Design

Markov cohort state transition model of perinatal and childhood HBV infection.

Data sources

Published data on maternal HBV prevalence (0.4%) and hepatitis B surface antigen testing (99.5% sensitivity), childhood vaccine completion (universal birth-dose strategy: 91.1%; deferred strategy: 87.1%; shared decision-making strategy: 50.0%), and age-stratified risk for chronic HBV infection.

Target population

One-year birth cohort of U.S.-born infants (n = 3.6 million).

Time horizon

20 years.

Intervention

Universal birth-dose vaccination, deferred (2-month) vaccination, and vaccination through shared decision making.

Outcome measures

Numbers with chronic HBV infection and susceptibility to HBV, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) derived from probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Results of base-case analysis

Compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (255 childhood infections [95% UI, 130 to 530]), the deferred and shared decision-making strategies would increase chronic HBV infections in the 2026 birth cohort by 19% to 303 (95% UI, 155 to 610) and by 83% to 467 (95% UI, 209 to 1032), respectively. These strategies would also increase the number of HBV-susceptible people at year 20 (474 000 and 1 806 000) compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (232 000).

Results of sensitivity analysis

In a scenario with lower vaccine coverage (84.5%) and higher HBV prevalence (maternal prevalence of 0.72% and higher risk for horizontal infection), chronic HBV infections would increase to 1700 and 2192, respectively, with the deferred and shared decision-making strategies.

Limitation

Uncertainty in horizontal HBV infection risk.

Conclusion

Proposed policy changes for vaccination through shared decision making are projected to result in an 83% increase in childhood HBV infections, and between 50% and 70% of children entering adulthood annually would be susceptible to HBV infection. Policymakers should reimplement recommendations for universal birth-dose vaccination.

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

summary: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, yet the real-world performance of FDA-cleared AI detection models remains incompletely characterized. We retrospectively evaluated two FDA-cleared AI algorithms from a single commercial platform (Aidoc Medical BriefCase)—one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA; n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE (iPE) detection on routine contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 37,191), across a 17-facility academic health system. Reference-standard labels were extracted from radiology reports using a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, κ = 0.94). The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity, with sensitivity declining from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE. The iPE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity. Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.

summary: Evaluation of AI-generated patient communication lacks standardized frameworks, and automated metrics may not reflect clinical utility. We leveraged a staged rollout of GPT-generated draft responses (GDRs) to patient portal messages. Thirty primary care physicians received drafts from September 2023 to August 2024 under two conditions: an intervention group where AI drafts were displayed and edited (n = 21,073), and a non-displayed group where drafts were generated but never shown to physicians, who composed responses independently (n = 45,127). We evaluated messages using BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and Flesch Reading Ease, and then correlated automated metrics with blinded physician ratings of effectiveness, misunderstanding potential, and harm. In the intervention group, 2264 (11%) drafts were incorporated into final messages with high semantic alignment (BERTScore F1 = 0.93). In the non-displayed group, independent physician messages showed moderate similarity to unseen drafts (BERTScore F1 = 0.83). Despite comparable semantic scores, physicians preferred human-authored messages (4.24/5). BERTScore correlated with physician quality ratings in the intervention group but not in the non-displayed. Automated metrics demonstrated context-dependent validity; they assessed editing fidelity but failed to evaluate whether AI-generated content matches independent human performance. Rigorous evaluation of clinical generative AI requires validation of metric meaning within specific use contexts.
title: Silent evaluation reveals context-dependent validity of automated metrics for AI-generated clinical messages

summary:
Importance

International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Objective

To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Design, setting, and participants

This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025.

Intervention

Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention.

Results

Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone.

Conclusions and relevance

Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06462313.
title: Intraoperative Dobutamine Plus Norepinephrine to Prevent Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Septic Shock: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary: Quadruplet therapy, combining anti-CD38 antibodies, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors and dexamethasone, is now the standard induction treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). However, treatment response is heterogeneous and molecular predictors are needed to guide early therapeutic decisions. We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of 423 tumor samples from patients with NDMM from the MIDAS cohort to characterize molecular heterogeneity and its association with measurable residual disease (MRD) after quadruplet induction with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (Isa-KRd). Postinduction MRD-negativity rates varied significantly across gene expression subtypes, with HP1/HP3 and MS groups showing superior responses compared to the MF and CD2 subtypes. B cell differentiation was associated with MRD positivity, while proliferation and MYC programs were associated with MRD negativity. These MRD-associated transcriptomic features were independently validated in the CASSIOPEIA cohort. Whole-genome sequencing revealed both known (APOBEC mutagenesis, chromothripsis) and new genomic instability phenotypes validated in the MMRF cohort. New driver alterations were identified with independent validation across three external cohorts with multiple myeloma (MMRF, MANHATTAN and CASSIOPEIA; 1,451 cases). Genomic instability features and driver genes such as CCND1 and MYC correlated with differential MRD outcomes. DNA methylation profiling identified nine MRD-linked subgroups distinguished by the extent of hypomethylation in quiescent chromatin and cis/trans signatures of driver translocations. A multimodal random forest model integrating genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features predicted MRD status after induction, with an area under the curve of 0.77, outperforming clinical and genomic models, while providing comparable discrimination and improved calibration relative to the transcriptomic and epigenomic models. These findings define a multiomic classification of NDMM linked to Isa-KRd response. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04934475 . In a multiomic analysis of samples from patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone induction therapy followed by consolidation treatment guided by minimal residual disease (MRD) status, baseline genomic, transcriptomic and epigenetic features are associated with MRD status after induction.
title: Molecular predictors of minimal residual disease in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with quadruplet therapy

summary: Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0–128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4–174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease study showed that while global trends in pertussis (whooping cough) declined from 1990 to 2023, the rebound in incidence and mortality since 2020, particularly in high-income regions, reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.
title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study

summary:
Background

Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study.

Methods

In a 26-week trial conducted at 22 primary care practices in the United States, we randomly assigned adults with type 2 diabetes who were not using insulin to either CGM or routine care (control). The primary outcome was the glycated hemoglobin level at 26 weeks. Key CGM-measured secondary outcomes were tested hierarchically to control the type I error rate.

Results

A total of 145 participants were assigned to the CGM group, and 138 to the routine-care group. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 84 years. The mean (±SD) glycated hemoglobin level decreased from 8.8±1.3% at baseline to 7.2±1.1% at 26 weeks in the CGM group and from 8.7±1.2% to 8.0±1.4% in the routine-care group (adjusted mean difference, -0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.1 to -0.6; P<0.001). The mean percentage of time that the CGM-measured glucose level was in the glucose-level range of 70 to 180 mg per deciliter was 21 percentage points higher (95% CI, 16 to 26) with CGM than with routine care (P<0.001). The between-group difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 54 mg per deciliter was -0.17 percentage points (95% CI, -0.27 to -0.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority); the difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 70 mg per deciliter was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.004 for superiority). No severe hypoglycemia events were reported.

Conclusions

Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care. (Funded by Dexcom; CONNECT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06601166.).
title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Non-Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes.

Background

Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.

Objective

To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment rates after diagnoses.

Design

Cohort study.

Setting

Population-based.

Participants

Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Measurements

Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based visits) were examined. Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.

Results

Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home HRAs increased between 2018 and 2022 for hypertension (45.9% to 47.7%), hyperlipidemia (57.8% to 66.7%), diabetes (47.8% to 51.6%), atrial fibrillation (30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.

Limitations

Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter settings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Conclusion

Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after facility-based encounters.

Primary funding source

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

summary: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in managing lower-grade glioma (LGG), but its response varies widely. Reliable pre-treatment prediction of RT response could facilitate patient management but remains unavailable. Here we present GUARD-LGG, a machine learning model designed to predict early RT response in LGG before treatment. GUARD-LGG was trained on 963 patients from a major center, tested on 187 patients from seven independent institutions, and 328 patients prospectively enrolled in a registered clinical trial. GUARD-LGG achieved AUCs of 0.946 (95% CI: 0.938–0.962), 0.929 (95% CI: 0.894–0.965), 0.882 (95% CI: 0.830–0.934), and 0.913 (95% CI: 0.878–0.949) in the training, internal validation, external, and prospective test sets, respectively. Model interpretation highlighted residual tumor, age, T2-weighted texture roughness and T1-weighted contrast intensity changes as major predictors. Radiogenomic analyses suggested potential associations between predicted unfavorable RT response and enrichment of RT resistance-related pathways. Consistently, patients with predicted unfavorable RT response exhibited shorter overall survival. In conclusion, GUARD-LGG enables individualized prediction of early RT response before therapy, offering a tool for pre-treatment response stratification in LGG.

summary: Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. summary:
Importance

Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown.

Objective

To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults.

Design, setting, and participants

International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU.

Exposures

Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation.

Main outcomes and measures

Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation.

Results

Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix.

Conclusions and relevance

In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.
title: Fluid Therapy in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Adult Patients.

summary:
Importance

It remains unclear if intraoperative hemodynamic therapy should be guided by cardiac index.

Objective

To evaluate whether individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy vs routine hemodynamic therapy improves outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial enrolled high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery between October 8, 2023, and October 25, 2025, at 12 university medical centers in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, and Spain. The date of last follow-up was January 15, 2026.

Interventions

Patients were randomized to individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index vs routine hemodynamic therapy (with blinded cardiac index monitoring).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was a composite of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.

Results

Of the 1128 patients enrolled, 1111 were randomized and 1095 were included in the primary analysis (median age, 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 49.4% were female). The primary outcome occurred in 243 of 549 patients (44.3%) in the individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy group vs 256 of 546 patients (46.9%) in the routine hemodynamic therapy group (relative risk, 0.94 [95.1% CI, 0.83-1.08]; P = .38). There were no between-group differences for the incidence of the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days.

Conclusions and relevance

Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05648279.
title: Individualized Cardiac Index-Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery: The PELICAN Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Objective

To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines.

Design

Systematic review and meta-research analysis.

Data sources

Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome.

Main outcome measures

Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness.

Results

The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare.

Conclusion

Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.
title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review.

summary:
Importance

The optimal vasopressor dose at which to initiate a second vasopressor in patients with septic shock is uncertain.

Objective

To compare the effects of hospital-level strategies initiating vasopressin infusion at a lower threshold vs a higher threshold on outcomes in patients with septic shock.

Design, setting, and participants

Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026.

Intervention

Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics.

Results

There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]).

Conclusions and relevance

In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06217562.
title: Effect of Vasopressin Initiation Threshold on Septic Shock Mortality: The VASSPR Cluster Crossover Randomized Strategy Trial.

summary: Medicare Part D 2027 National Average Monthly Bid Amount Information On July 28, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released preliminary technical Medicare Part D bid information for contract year (CY) 2027 to help Part D plan sponsors finalize their Part D and Medicare Advantage (MA) offerings and prepare for Medicare Open Enrollment. Additionally, CMS is announcing the conclusion of the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration, a voluntary demonstration for standalone prescription drug plans implemented in CY 2025 to address volatility and variation in standalone premiums following benefit changes mandated by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). For CY 2027, CMS bid analysis indicates that Part D plan sponsors had sufficient experience under the redesigned Part D benefit to support their assumptions in developing the prescription drug plan bids. Therefore, CMS will discontinue the demonstration at the end of CY 2026 to return the program to operating under traditional market conditions in CY 2027. As in past years, CMS will release the 2027 MA and Part D landscape in mid-to-late September, once all offerings are finalized. In addition, CMS will release final average MA and Part D premiums, along with other key information, in September with the MA and Part D landscape. National Average Monthly Bid Amount and Government Subsidy The national average monthly bid amount (NAMBA) is an enrollment-weighted average of all applicable Part D plan bids for basic Part D benefits, with weights based on the number of enrollees in each plan. The NAMBA is used to calculate the government subsidy for plans. In 2027, the NAMBA will be $296.05. Base Beneficiary Premium for 2027 The national base beneficiary premium is the starting point for calculating a plan-specific basic Part D premium. This value is calculated per a statutory formula, using a percentage of bids and estimates of reinsurance costs submitted by certain Part D plans for the required statutory minimum level of coverage (known as the “basic” benefit). Between 2024 and 2029, the annual increase in the base beneficiary premium is capped by the IRA’s premium stabilization provision not to exceed 6% per year. For 2027, the base beneficiary premium will be $41.33. ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary: Fiscal Year 2027 Medicare Inpatient Psychiatric Facility Prospective Payment System Final Rule (CMS-1847-F) On July 29, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule to update Medicare payment policies and rates for Inpatient Psychiatric Facilities (IPFs) under the IPF Prospective Payment System (PPS) (CMS-1847-F) for fiscal year (FY) 2027. CMS is publishing this final rule consistent with its statutory authority to update Medicare payment policies for IPFs annually. This fact sheet discusses the provisions of the final rule, including annual updates to the prospective payment rates, the outlier threshold, the wage index, and associated impact analysis. In addition, the rule finalizes a policy effective for FY 2028 (October 1, 2027) to limit outlier payments at the facility level to no more than 20% of an IPF’s total IPF PPS payments in a year, for IPFs with at least 50 stays per year. For the IPF Quality Reporting Program, CMS is removing two measures from the program, as well as implementing a standardized IPF patient assessment instrument. Changes to Payments Under the IPF PPS Updates to IPF Payment Rates For FY 2027, CMS is updating the IPF PPS payment rates by 2.3%, based on the 2021-based IPF market basket increase of 3.2% less a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment. Additionally, CMS is updating the outlier threshold so that estimated outlier payments remain at 2% of total IPF PPS payments. Total estimated payments to IPFs would increase by 2.3%, or $60 million, in FY 2027, relative to IPF payments in FY 2026. Reform of IPF PPS Outlier Payment Policy The IPF PPS includes an outlier adjustment to promote access to IPF care for those patients who require expensive care and to limit the financial risk of IPFs treating unusually costly patients. Providing additional payments to IPFs for extremely costly cases strongly improves the accuracy of the IPF PPS in determining resource costs at the patient and facility level. Outlier payments are determined by comparing the estimated cost of an IPF stay to a threshold value. The outlier fixed dollar loss threshold is set each year so that estimated outlier payments equal 2% of total IPF PPS payments. In recent years, the outlier threshold has increased significantly, and commenters have expressed concerns that it is increasingly difficult to receive outlier payments for costly IPF stays. Our analysis of IPF PPS outlier payments has shown that certain IPFs have exceptionally high reported costs and receive outlier payments on many of their claims. We note that these providers’ high overall costs are primarily driven by high routine costs (for example, labor, real estate, or overhead), which are fixed at the provider level and do not vary from one patient to another. We are finalizing the proposal to cap outlier payments at the provider level to minimize the impact of these high-cost facilities on the outlier pool. However, we are deferring the effective date of this policy until FY 2028 to provide additional time to evaluate the cost drivers identified by commenters. In addition, we are finalizing an exception to this cap policy for facilities with fewer than 50 stays per year. Updates to the IPF Quality Reporting Program The IPF Quality Reporting Program requires that all IPFs paid under the IPF PPS submit certain specified quality data to CMS, in a form and manner and within the timeframes that CMS prescribes. IPFs that do not submit the specified data on quality measures as required by the IPF Quality Reporting Program receive a 2-percentage-point reduction to their annual payment update. The IPF Quality Reporting Program aims to assess and improve the quality of care provided to IPF patients. By requiring IPFs to submit quality data to CMS and by CMS publicly reporting such data under the IPF Quality Reporting Program, CMS ensures that patients can make more informed decisions about their healthcare options. In this final rule, CMS is making changes to quality measures in the IPF Quality Reporting Program. CMS is removing two measures beginning with the CY 2026 reporting period/FY 2028 payment determination: the Alcohol Use Brief Intervention Provided or Offered (SUB-2) and subset Alcohol Use Brief Intervention (SUB-2a) measure and the Tobacco Use Treatment Provided or Offered at Discharge (TOB-3) and subset Tobacco Use Treatment at Discharge (TOB-3a) measure. CMS is also implementing a standardized IPF patient assessment instrument (IPF-PAI), as mandated by section 4125(b)(1) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (CAA, 2023). IPFs will have two methods to submit IPF-PAI data to CMS. IPFs can use a free CMS-developed web application called the Patient Assessment Reporting Interoperability Tool (PARIT) or can submit IPF-PAI data using Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) CMS has built from the Health Level Seven (HL7®) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®) specification. This will be the first CMS statutory quality reporting program to use the FHIR standard to support patient assessment data submission. The final rule can be viewed at the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/current . Information on the Inpatient Psychiatric Facility PPS is available at: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/inpatient-psychiatric-facility . Information on the Inpatient Psychiatric Facility Quality Reporting Program is available at: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/quality/initiatives/hospital-quality-initiative/inpatient-psychiatric-facility-quality-reporting-ipfqr-program . ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary: Fiscal Year 2027 Skilled Nursing Facility Prospective Payment System Final Rule (CMS 1843-F) On July 29, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule for updates to Medicare payment policies and rates for skilled nursing facilities under the Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF) Prospective Payment System (PPS) for fiscal year (FY) 2027. CMS is publishing this final rule consistent with the legal requirements to update Medicare payment policies for SNFs annually. This fact sheet discusses the final rule’s provisions. FY 2027 Final Updates to the SNF Payment Rates For FY 2027, CMS finalized updating SNF PPS rates by 2.4% based on the final SNF market basket of 3.3%, reduced by a 0.9% productivity adjustment, for an estimated increase of $882.74 million in aggregate payments to SNFs. FY 2027 Final Updates to the SNF Quality Reporting Program Measure Removal. CMS is finalizing the removal of two measures from the SNF Quality Reporting Program ( QRP), beginning with the FY 2028 SNF QRP: (1) the COVID-19 Vaccination Coverage Among Healthcare Personnel measure, and (2) the COVID-19 Vaccine: Percent of Patients/Residents Who Are Up to Date measure. Data Submission Deadline. CMS is finalizing the revised data submission timeframe from 4.5 months to approximately 45 days, beginning with the FY 2029 SNF QRP. This shortened timeframe will reduce the lag between data submission and public reporting by up to three months, resulting in timelier data for consumers and their families. SNFs will also have earlier access to data to support their quality initiatives. Minimum Data Set ( MDS) Data Submission. To obtain the most accurate SNF quality of care information and to remain relevant to the SNF community and consumers, CMS is finalizing a requirement for all SNFs to submit MDS data for all SNF residents receiving covered skilled care, regardless of payer. This will align the SNF QRP with other Post-Acute Care settings and CMS programs that already collect data on all patients regardless of payer. FY 2027 SNF QRP Request for Information CMS received comments on one potential measure topic that might be adopted in future years for the SNF QRP: advanced care planning (ACP). ACP is a continuous process of conversation and documentation to align a patient’s care and interventions with their beliefs, values, and preferences if they become unable to make those decisions. CMS provides a summary of comments received in the FY 2027 SNF PPS final rule. FY 2027 Final Updates to the SNF Value-Based Purchasing Program For the SNF Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) Program, CMS finalized performance standards for the FY 2029 and FY 2030 program years to comply with the program’s statutory notice deadline. CMS will update the “snapshot date” codified at 42 CFR § 413.338(f)(1)(v) for two measures calculated using MDS assessment data to maintain alignment with the newly finalized SNF QRP submission deadlines for MDS assessment data, beginning with FY 2027 data. The SNF VBP adjustments for certain SNFs subject to the net reduction in payments under the SNF VBP and which are not incorporated into the impact estimates for the payment rate are an estimated $203.60 million reduction in FY 2027. Request for Information on Updating the Patient Driven Payment Model Payment System to Address Case-Mix Upcoding This Request for Information (RFI) focused on potential updates to the Patient Driven Payment Model payment system as part of a broader effort to ensure that payment policy reflects current care practices and changes in the SNF resident population. The RFI also focused on how CMS could address observed case-mix upcoding. CMS will take the comments received under advisement in any potential proposed adjustments in future rulemaking. The SNF Prospective Payment System Final Rule can be viewed on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/current CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary: Fiscal Year 2027 Hospice Wage Index and Payment Rate Update and Hospice Quality Reporting Program Requirements Final Rule (CMS-1851-F) On July 30, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule (CMS-1851-F) that would update Medicare hospice payments and the aggregate cap amount for fiscal year (FY) 2027 under existing statutory and regulatory requirements. This final rule also highlights Medicare non-hospice spending under a hospice election, using data from the hospice service and spending variation index (SSVI). The SSVI includes a comprehensive scoring system calculated using nine claims-based measures, each representing a different aspect of hospice utilization as well as non-hospice spending. These data indicate hospice providers that might need additional targeted education and oversight. This rule also finalizes changes to the hospice election statement regulations; these regulations require hospices to provide to all Medicare beneficiaries, at the time of hospice election, an addendum to the election statement regarding coverage of non-hospice services. Additionally, this rule finalizes conforming regulation text changes that allow a physician designee and the physician member of the interdisciplinary group, in addition to the hospice medical director, to discharge a patient from hospice care, which will help improve flexibility for hospices and reduce regulatory burden. This rule also finalizes conforming regulation text changes to the hospice telehealth face-to-face policy under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026. The final rule includes a summary of comments from requests for information on enhancing community palliative care services under current Medicare benefits; developing a hospice-specific wage index using BLS data; and describing any experiences with overlap between hospice and assisted suicide or “medical aid in dying.” FY 2027 Routine Annual Rate Setting Changes For FY 2027, CMS updated the hospice payment rate by 2.3% (an estimated increase of $755 million in payments from FY 2026). This figure results from the finalized 3.2% inpatient hospital market basket percentage increase reduced, as required by law, by a finalized 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment. The finalized FY 2027 rates for hospices that do not submit required quality data information include the finalized FY 2027 hospice payment update percentage of 2.3% minus four percentage points as required by law, which would result in a 1.7% reduction over the previous year’s payment rate. These finalized payment rates reflect the most accurate, updated data available on the cost of goods, services, and labor. Hospice payments are subject to a statutory aggregate cap limiting the overall payments made to a hospice annually. The finalized hospice cap amount for FY 2027 is $36,174.75 (FY 2026 cap amount of $35,361.44 increased by the FY 2027 hospice payment update percentage of 2.3%). Service and Spending Variation Index Given the growing concern of fraud, waste, and abuse in hospice care, CMS has continued to monitor trends on a variety of metrics from hospice claims, including non-hospice spending during a hospice election. CMS’ internal monitoring has identified patterns of hospice care delivery and associated non-hospice spending per hospice day. The comprehensive services covered under the Medicare hospice benefit are structured so that hospice beneficiaries do not have to routinely seek items, services, or drugs beyond those provided by hospice. CMS continues to believe that it would be unusual and exceptional to see services provided outside of hospice for those individuals approaching the end of life and has reiterated since 1983 that “virtually all” care needed by the terminally ill would be provided by the hospice. However, CMS has seen non-hospice spending continue to rise in recent years. In response, CMS developed a service and spending variation index (SSVI), using metrics collected from claims data, that can signal potentially inappropriate utilization or concerns with quality of care or compliance. The SSVI uses a scoring system, with a higher score representing potential concerning hospice utilization and non-hospice spending. This information provides transparency for CMS data analysis, can help beneficiaries make informed decisions, and could support program integrity efforts. CMS solicited comments on the metrics and the SSVI scoring system and summarizes those comments in this final rule. Additionally, this final rule discusses the SSVI, which includes data from FYs 2024 and 2025, displays provider-level data, and includes each hospice’s SSVI score. This final rule uses more recent claims data to update the SSVI, though no substantive changes to the methodology were made. To view the SSVI scores for FYs 2024 and 2025, additional data from claims-based measures, and related documentation on the methodology, visit: https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-15686 . Finalized Mandatory Hospice Election Statement Addendum The hospice election statement addendum is a written addendum to a Medicare hospice election statement that lists and explains what conditions, items, services, or drugs the hospice has determined are not related to the beneficiary’s terminal illness and related conditions — and will therefore not be covered under the Medicare hospice benefit. In the FY 2020 Hospice Final Rule (84 FR 38484), CMS finalized the requirement that a hospice provide a hospice election statement addendum to a beneficiary upon request to increase coverage transparency and potentially help ensure that Medicare beneficiaries who elect the hospice benefit are provided comprehensive and holistic services. Hospices are also required to provide the hospice election statement addendum to requesting non-hospice providers who furnish services to a beneficiary under hospice. Despite this addendum requirement being finalized in FY 2020, Medicare non-hospice spending for beneficiaries who have elected the hospice benefit has shown substantial and consistent growth from FY 2020 through FY 2024, with particularly dramatic increases in Part A and B spending. This may suggest that the policy requirement stipulating that hospices only provide the addendum to beneficiaries (or their representatives) that request it — rather than every beneficiary who elects the benefit — has not achieved the intended accountability objective of ensuring that hospices provide virtually all care needed by terminally ill individuals as required under the comprehensive and holistic Medicare hospice benefit. Additionally, many beneficiaries or their representatives may not realize the importance of asking for the addendum and may continue to bear more financial burden as a result. In this final rule, CMS made the addendum mandatory for all those electing hospice and not just those who request the addendum. This change ensures that all beneficiaries have greater transparency into non-covered items, services, or drugs to make care decisions that align with their treatment preferences and goals, potentially leading to a decrease in beneficiary out-of-pocket costs. This requirement may hold hospices more accountable for the items, services, and drugs they are required to provide. The addendum also will provide needed information to non-hospice providers for claims submission. Hospice Quality Reporting Program The Secretary, authorized by Section 1814(i)(5) of the Social Security Act, established the hospice quality reporting requirements for hospice programs and is also required to publicly report quality measures that relate to the care provided by hospice programs across the country on https://www.medicare.gov/care-compare/ . Since FY 2014, the failure of hospices to comply with quality data reporting requirements results in a two percentage-point reduction to the annual payment update (APU) for the corresponding FY. In the FY 2022 Hospice Final Rule, CMS finalized that beginning with the FY 2024 APU and for each subsequent year, under statute, the APU penalty increased from two percentage points to four percentage points for hospices that did not comply with the Hospice Quality Reporting Program (HQRP). Despite the doubling of the APU penalty increase in FY 2024, CMS has not seen significant improvement in the number of hospices meeting the HQRP reporting requirements. In FY 2024, the first year of the percentage points APU penalty, 22.06% of hospices were found to be non-compliant. In FY 2025, the percentage of non-compliant hospices increased to 23.53%, and in FY 2026 the percentage of non-compliant hospices was 20.37%. The consistent lack of data for approximately one-fifth of hospices limits CMS’ ability to accurately measure the quality of care provided by hospices and reduces the amount of data available to consumers. In this rule, CMS will add an icon to the Medicare.gov Care Compare tool to identify hospices that fail to submit any quality data, or submit less than the required 90%, within a given year — effective no earlier than FY 2028. To comply, hospices must submit quality data through the Hospice Outcomes and Patient Evaluation (HOPE) tool within 30 days of the patient's HOPE admission, HOPE Update Visit (HUV), and HOPE discharge dates. ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary: FY 2027 Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRF) Prospective Payment System (PPS) Final Rule (CMS-1845-F) On July 30, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that updates Medicare payment policies and rates for inpatient rehabilitation facilities under the Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRF) Prospective Payment System (PPS) and the IRF Quality Reporting Program (QRP) for fiscal year (FY) 2027. CMS is publishing this final rule consistent with the legal requirements to update Medicare payment policies for IRFs annually. For FY 2027, CMS finalized an update to the IRF PPS payment rates of 2. 3 % based on an IRF market basket update of 3.2%, less a 0. 9 percentage point productivity adjustment. The final rule includes annual updates to the prospective payment rates, the outlier threshold, the case-mix-group relative weights and average length of stay values, the wage index, and associated impact analysis. In addition, this final rule includes policy revisions for the 36-hour rule (§ 412.622(a)(3)(ii)), updates to the interdisciplinary team meeting (IDT) 412.622(a)(5)(ii)), and provides a summary of feedback on one Request for Information (RFI) on payment reform. The IRF QRP is a pay-for-reporting program. IRFs that do not meet reporting requirements are subject to a 2-percentage-point reduction in their Annual Increase Factor. Additionally, measures adopted into the IRF QRP are publicly reported on the Care Compare tool at Medicare.gov. In the FY 2027 IRF PPS rule, CMS is finalizing a revised data submission deadline for the IRF QRP and providing a summary of feedback on one RFI . Updates to the FY 2027 IRF PPS Payment Rates For FY 2027, CMS finalized an update to the IRF PPS payment rates by 2.3% based on the IRF market basket percentage increase of 3.2%, less a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment based on more recent data that became available after the publication of the proposed rule. This final rule also applies to the third and final year of the phase-out of the rural adjustment for IRFs transitioning from rural to urban (which began in FY 2025) that were reclassified due to updated Core-Based Statistical Area delineations. Additionally, CMS finalized the outlier threshold to maintain outlier payments at 3% of total payments. CMS estimates the final technical rate setting changes would result in an estimated increase in IRF payments of $340 million for FY 2027. Final Updates to FY 2027 IRF PPS Payment CMS finalized a revision to § 412.622(a)(3)(ii) to specify that all (not just some) therapies must be initiated within 36 hours of admission to the IRF . CMS believes this revision will significantly reduce inquiries and support the IRF industry. CMS also finalized a revision to the current IDT policy (§ 412.622(a)(5)(ii)) to mandate that the initial meeting is completed on or before the fourth day of admission to align with the plan of care, and clarify that subsequent IDT meetings are conducted weekly (with CMS defining “weekly” as seven days from the date of the initial IDT meeting, that must occur by day four), which enhances the ongoing development and execution of the patient’s plan of care. Proposed Updates to the FY 2027 IRF QRP Data Submission Deadline: CMS is finalizing the revision to shorten the timeframe for data submission from 4.5 months to approximately 45 days beginning with the FY 2029 IRF QRP. This new timeframe would reduce the lag between data submission and public reporting by up to three months, resulting in timelier data for consumers and their families. IRFs will also have earlier access to data to support their quality initiatives. IRF PPS and QRP Requests for Information CMS sought feedback on potential enhancements to the IRF PPS, including updates to how primary diagnoses and comorbidities are used to classify patients by case mix. These potential updates would build on selected elements of the case-mix classification methodology used in the Skilled Nursing Facility Patient Driven Payment Model, as implemented in the FY 2019 final rule, and would move IRF payment toward a more robust, modernized system better aligned with other post-acute payment systems settings. CMS received comments on one potential measure topic that CMS is considering adopting in future years for the IRF QRP: advanced care planning (ACP). ACP is a continuous process of conversation and documentation to align a patient’s care and interventions with their beliefs, values, and preferences, if they become unable to make those decisions. CMS provides a summary of comments received in the FY 2027 IRF PPS final rule. Finalized Change to the Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS) Competitive Bidding Program (CBP) As part of the FY 2027 IRF PPS final rule, CMS finalized the update to the DMEPOS Competitive Bidding Program’s bid surety bond requirements. The final change increases the bid surety bond amount from $50,000 to $100,000 for bids submitted under a Remote Item Delivery (RID) Competitive Bidding Program (CBP) and requires only one $100,000 bid surety bond per bidding entity, regardless of how many competitions under the RID CBP it bids on. For all other competitions, the bid surety bond amount remains $50,000, and bidding entities must obtain a separate bid surety bond for each competitive bidding area. This change aims to deter bidders from submitting disingenuous bids. CMS has launched the first phase of its Round 2028 DMEPOS CBP bidder education initiative. This early education phase provides prospective DMEPOS suppliers with important information about the upcoming bidding process, eligibility requirements, and key program changes before the registration and bidding periods open, giving them ample time to prepare. For more information, review the Round 2028 bidder education materials and Frequently Asked Questions , and sign up for the Competitive Bidding Implementation Contractor’s listserv at: www.dmecompetitivebid.com . The final rule can be viewed at the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/current . For more information about IRF QRP, please visit: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/quality/inpatient-rehabilitation-facility For more information about IRF PPS, please visit: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/inpatient-rehabilitation ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
