summary:
Importance

Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited.

Objective

To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries.

Design, setting, and participants

This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries.

Main outcomes and measures

The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined.

Results

Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians.

Conclusions and relevance

Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.
title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.

summary: Background: Regulatory frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Common Rule, and the Declaration of Helsinki require informed consent to ensure participants understand a study’s purpose and can make voluntary decisions about their involvement. Regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation [EU] 2016/679), further emphasize that consent must be freely given and revocable without disadvantage. Although informed consent forms (ICFs) are intended to be clear and accessible, they have become increasingly lengthy and complex. Large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to navigate and interpret this complexity and have shown promise in biomedical information extraction tasks. However, their susceptibility to hallucinations limits their reliability in high-stakes settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can mitigate such errors. Objective: This study evaluates the integration of GPT-4.1 with RAG for reviewing data reuse language in ICFs and its ability to interpret complex ICF language. Methods: First, we processed 438 ICFs from different trials, including multiple countries, languages, and versions of ICFs. Using expertly curated prompts, we extracted information about data reuse using GPT-4.1. By comparing the LLM-generated data reuse outputs with human expert ground truth, we evaluated accuracy and the time required to extract information for each ICF. To further validate the workflow, we evaluated an independent set of 488 ICFs spanning additional trials, languages, and regions. During the validation phase, the workflow was evaluated using a baseline assessment (89 ICFs) followed by 3 iterative optimization rounds assessed on 14, 281, and 104 ICFs, respectively. For this cohort, we assessed the correctness of LLM outputs along with the quality of supporting evidence provided by the model. Results: Across the initial set of 438 ICFs, the system achieved 81.6% accuracy. During validation, the baseline accuracy using the preoptimized prompts was 84.0% (89 documents). Accuracy improved sequentially across the 3 iterative optimization rounds, increasing from 82.3% in the first round (14 documents) to 90.7% in the second round (281 documents), and reaching 92.1% in the third and final round on an independent holdout cohort of 104 documents. Ultimately, using our RAG-based approach, the system accurately extracted data reuse information across multiple languages. Conclusions: Our RAG-based workflow demonstrated the ability to effectively support the ICF review process for data reuse and interpret complex consent language, contributing to improved consistency in ICF evaluations for data reuse.
title: Large Language Model–Assisted Review of Clinical Trial Informed Consent for Data Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach

summary: This letter comments on the systematic review and meta-analysis of large language models (LLMs) in mental health care by Leung and colleagues (JMIR AI 2026;5:e87730). The bivariate meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustments is methodologically sound, and its cautious conclusions are warranted. I raise an unaddressed threat to the pooled estimates: model version drift. Over the search window (November 2022 to March 2026), "GPT-4" did not denote a single intervention; released in March 2023, it was followed by API snapshots whose behavior differed materially, with accuracy on a prime-number identification task falling from 84% to 51% between the March and June 2023 versions. Because the review extracted only model name and model type and did not capture version or testing dates, the estimates pooled under GPT-4 (k=4) and GPT-3.5 (k=4) may each span several substantively different models, and the pooled GPT-4 estimate may correspond to no single system a clinician could deploy. This concern is distinct from the acknowledged limitation that few studies evaluated the newest variants, which concerns currency rather than comparability. I suggest reporting model version and testing date for each pooled study (consistent with TRIPOD-LLM item 6a), examining robustness to version mixing in sensitivity analyses, and qualifying the abstract comparative statements accordingly.
title: Same Name, Moving Target: Model Version Drift in Syntheses of Large Language Models for Mental Health

summary: The proliferation of evaluative approaches for generative AI tools used for mental health purposes reflects much-needed attention to safety, ethics, and emerging risks. However, limited alignment across frameworks complicates comparisons, slows progress toward shared goals, and provides little clarity for regulatory processes. The result is a fragmented field that lacks cohesive guidance as the technology and its real-world patterns of use continue to evolve. This position paper synthesizes current evaluative approaches, outlines sources of divergence across existing frameworks, and identifies shared domains that could serve as anchors for coordinated development. We advocate for a living, flexible meta-framework maintained by a global, cross-sector consortium that can harmonize criteria, support consistent evaluation across jurisdictions, and adapt alongside scientific, clinical, and technological advances. Such a structure can strengthen safety, transparency, and methodological consistency while giving researchers, clinicians, developers, and policymakers a shared foundation for assessing generative AI tools in mental health care.
title: Toward a Living Meta-Framework for Evaluating Generative AI in Mental Health

summary: Background: Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective: This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods: This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results: Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions: Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.
title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings

summary: Background: Telemedicine has emerged as a critical strategy to address health care access gaps in hard-to-reach areas, particularly in resource-constrained settings. While telemedicine services have expanded across India, evidence on post-implementation experiences, specifically regarding the integration of portable diagnostic tools, and the assisting role of frontline health care workers, remains limited. Understanding these sociotechnical dynamics is essential for optimizing digital health interventions in remote areas. Objective: This study aimed to explore perceptions, experiences, and implementation processes of an assisted telemedicine model where frontline health care workers facilitate real-time, doorstep patient-assisted-to-doctor consultations using portable diagnostics and a customized portal among health care workers and patients in hard-to-reach villages of Rajasthan, India. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in 5 remote villages of Balotra district, Rajasthan, between December 2025 and January 2026, following a 10-month telemedicine intervention. In-depth, semistructured interviews were conducted with 28 participants, including medical officers (n=3, 10.71%), nurses, and accredited social health activists or auxiliary nurse midwives (n=10, 35.71%), and patients (n=15, 53.57%). Cadre-specific semistructured interview guides were developed using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and Technology Acceptance Model. Interviews were analyzed using a reflexive thematic analysis approach, incorporating both inductive and deductive coding approaches in NVivo 15 (Lumivero). Triangulation across participant groups and analytic perspectives was used to enhance credibility and trustworthiness. Results: The analysis revealed that the assisted telemedicine model fundamentally reconfigured treatment-seeking behavior by providing doorstep care, significantly reducing travel burdens, and out-of-pocket expenditures. Frontline health care workers acted as crucial sociotechnical mediators, bridging the digital divide and fostering patient trust, particularly among women and older adults. Health care providers reported increased clinical confidence and workflow efficiency, supported by real-time vital monitoring and cross-verification via digital chatbots. However, implementation was challenged by intermittent network connectivity, diagnostic limitations for conditions requiring physical palpation, and occasional stock-outs of essential medicines. Despite these barriers, the gradual acceptance of the system was heavily facilitated by the continuous engagement and cultural mediation of local health workers. Conclusions: Telemedicine was perceived as a feasible and acceptable model for extending primary health care services in hard-to-reach areas, provided it is embedded within an assisted model supported by trained frontline workers and responsive technical systems. The findings emphasize the need to shift health care policy toward mediated-digital models, formally recognizing community health workers as digital health navigators. Future scale-up must prioritize strengthening rural digital infrastructure and ensuring a reliable supply chain for essential medicines to sustain long-term engagement and health equity. summary: Background: Clinicians spend a lot of time on electronic health record (EHR) documentation, often at the expense of direct patient interaction. Ambient listening technology uses AI to passively record and summarize clinical encounters. Although early studies are promising, there is limited evidence on system performance in complex, non-English settings. Objective: This study aimed to compare the documentation performance of 3 commercially available ambient listening systems in simulated Dutch-language outpatient consultations by assessing note completeness, correctness, and conciseness under predefined linguistic and interactional challenges. Methods: Standardized audio recordings of 10 scripted physician-patient interactions across 2 specialties were used. Scenarios included multispeaker dynamics (patient companion), conversational disruptions (nurse interruption), evasive patient communication, and a regional dialect (Gronings). Three ambient listening providers (provider 1, provider 2, and provider 3) processed the audio files. Generated notes were divided into 4 note sections: patient history, physical examination, diagnostic impression, and treatment plan. For each system output, each note section was scored for completeness, conciseness, and correctness using a 5-point ordinal scale against physician-developed reference summaries. In total, 8 clinicians participated in scoring: 4 junior clinicians evaluated all outputs, and 4 senior clinicians each reviewed a subset of scenarios. Analyses were based on 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores. Interrater agreement was assessed using Gwet agreement coefficient 2 (Gwet AC-2). System-level technical characteristics were assessed alongside clinical performance to aid interpretation of between-provider differences. Results: Across 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores on a 5-point scale, overall interrater agreement was high (Gwet AC-2=0.827). Provider-level mean scores ranged from 3.82 to 4.26 (4.26, SD 0.73 for provider 3, 4.00, SD 0.90 for provider 2, and 3.82, SD 1.07 for provider 1). Mean scores were higher in otolaryngology than in surgical oncology (4.36, SD 0.56 vs 3.68, SD 1.10). Across scoring domains, correctness received the highest mean score (4.21, SD 0.98), while completeness received the lowest (3.81, SD 0.90). Variation in mean scores was observed across script scenarios. Dialect-containing scenarios had the lowest mean score overall (3.77, SD 1.21), although this pattern was not uniform across specialties and systems. Median summary generation times ranged from 13.5 seconds (IQR 12-15; provider 3) to 22.0 seconds (IQR 18-24; provider 2). Conclusions: Ambient listening systems demonstrated generally strong performance in this simulated Dutch-language evaluation, including under several common conversational challenges. However, mean scores varied across scripted scenarios, with lower scores observed in some dialect-containing and otherwise challenging interactions. Future deployment studies must prioritize linguistic equity, real-world validation of efficiency gains, and evaluation of both clinician and patient perceptions to understand how these systems influence consultation dynamics and care delivery across diverse patient populations.
title: Three Ambient Listening Systems in Simulated Dutch-Language Multispeaker and Multidialect Clinical Encounters: Comparative Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. <strong>Methods:</strong> We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. <strong>Results:</strong> Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001 for all comparisons). In the supervised setting, Llama 3.1-8B fine-tuned on Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 81.43%, exceeding the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001) and achieving a numerically higher score than the substantially larger zero-shot Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct model (80.10%; <i>P</i>=.08). In contrast, traditional machine learning models and transformer encoders exhibited greater performance degradation under domain shift and derived limited benefit from increasing synthetic training data. Additional experiments showed that increasing synthetic training data improved cross-domain performance for LLM-based models but yielded comparatively smaller gains for traditional approaches. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Synthetic data generated by LLMs can serve as a scalable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving alternative to expert-annotated real-world clinical data for PPD from clinical text. The findings demonstrate successful cross-domain transfer to real-world US Department of Veterans Affairs clinical notes.
title: Large Language Model–Generated Synthetic Data for Parole and Probation Detection in Clinical Notes: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. Methods: KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and -score metrics. Results: Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and -score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. Conclusions: This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.
title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. <strong>Methods:</strong> We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. <strong>Results:</strong> Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub>=23.34; <i>P</i><.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant. Across 59 complete-panel cases, raw agreement was 79.0% (466/590 model-pair comparisons; 95% bootstrap CI 72.9%-84.7%), and Fleiss κ was 0.55 (95% bootstrap CI 0.43-0.66). Within-model response stability across 3 runs ranged from 85.0% (51/60) to 100.0% (59/59 and 60/60). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Selected contemporary LLMs showed model-dependent variation but moderate overall agreement in binary recommendations for medical ethics cases. These results characterize recommendation behavior under a fixed, time-specific protocol and do not establish ethical correctness or the effects on clinicians or patients. Reporting model version, recommendation tendency, confidence, and repeatability may improve transparency when such systems are evaluated for ethically sensitive applications.
title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study

summary: Background: Summary care records are digital technologies designed to support information sharing and care coordination across fragmented health and social care systems. However, adoption and use of these technologies can vary across diverse health and care settings, with users using workarounds and other strategies to meet their specific information needs. In Scotland, the Key Information Summary (KIS) has been in use for over 13 years, sharing key patient information from general practitioners (GPs) with other health and care providers for future care planning. Objective: Using the KIS as a case study, this study examines how various adoption strategies and workarounds have shaped the evolution of regional information infrastructures integrating health and social care in Scotland over time. Methods: This multimethod qualitative study examined the various contextual factors influencing adoption and use of the KIS across diverse health and care settings. Data collection included interviews with KIS users from health and care settings, implementers, and vendors; documentary analysis of user guides, websites, reports, and policies; and observation of multidisciplinary team meetings and technology use. Data analysis involved a hybrid approach. The technology-people-organization-macroenvironment framework was applied to code interview, documentary, and observational data, followed by an inductive analysis informed by science and technology studies theories of information infrastructures, domestication, and workarounds to examine strategies and workarounds for adapting the KIS to local contexts and evolving needs. Results: Data comprised 54 qualitative interviews, 59 documents, 2 websites, and 20 hours of observational field notes collected between April 2024 and March 2025. Findings indicate that adoption of the KIS varied across settings and over time due to misalignment between system design, evolving expectations of integrated care, and national initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic that repurposed its use. Professional roles and associated information needs shaped differing expectations of what constituted useful information, generating tensions between users who relied on the KIS and GPs responsible for maintaining it. Formal workarounds enabled the extension of the health care–centric infrastructure into nonclinical settings to facilitate information sharing with GPs and, in some cases, supported clinician access to the KIS during system outages. Across settings, informal user-driven repair practices enabled diverse professionals to adopt and realign the KIS with its intended use. Conclusions: This study demonstrates how regional information infrastructures integrating health and care evolve incrementally as they become embedded within local routines, practices, and existing systems. Adoption was shaped by professional roles, information needs, and users’ capabilities, with formal workarounds extending infrastructures into new settings and informal, user-driven repair practices supporting ongoing use and maintenance. Policymakers and vendors must recognize that workarounds and user-driven repair practices are central to infrastructural growth and sustainability, and understanding these strategies can inform future technology development and innovation.
title: Adoption Strategies and Workarounds in the Evolution of Information Infrastructures Integrating Health and Social Care Providers in Scotland: Multimethod Qualitative Case Study of the Key Information Summary

summary: Background: Mentalization is a core human capacity involving interpretation of one’s own and others’ behavior in terms of underlying mental states. Within the mentalization-based treatment (MBT) framework, it is described along multiple dimensions, integrating cognitive, affective, relational, and regulatory processes. Large language models (LLMs) can generate linguistically reflective discourse, raising the question of whether the formal linguistic structure of mentalization can be reproduced without experiential and affective processes. Objective: This study aimed to assess whether an LLM can generate mentalization profiles structurally coherent with MBT dimensions and recognized as formally mentalizing by expert clinicians. Specifically, it evaluated the structural and argumentative coherence of model-generated profiles and the level of agreement among MBT-trained psychiatrists. It also examined the distinction between psychological mentalization and algorithmic reflectivity, conceptualized as a formally coherent but nonexperiential linguistic phenomenon. Methods: A comparative, descriptive methodological design was adopted. A total of 50 human-model dialogues were generated under standardized conditions. At the end of each interaction, the model produced a narrative mentalization profile structured along MBT dimensions. Five MBT-trained psychiatrists independently evaluated each profile using anonymized materials. Ratings covered 4 canonical MBT axes and 2 additional higher-order dimensions—regulatory functions and synthetic profile. For each dimension, they assigned separate Likert-scale ratings for evaluative and argumentative coherence. Descriptive statistics were computed at dialogue level. Interrater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), primarily ICC(3,k), with CIs. The association between evaluative and argumentative coherence was examined using Pearson correlation coefficients with 95% CIs, with Spearman rank correlation as a robustness check. Results: Across dimensions, mean scores ranged from 3.63 (SD 0.63) to 3.98 (SD 0.31), indicating moderate-to-high structural coherence. Interrater reliability was moderate to good, with ICC(3,k) values ranging from 0.60 to 0.84 in the evaluative domain. The highest scores were observed for implicit-explicit and synthetic profile, whereas internal-external showed the lowest mean. Score distributions showed limited variability and concentration in the upper range of the scale. Evaluative and argumentative coherence were strongly associated across all MBT dimensions, with Pearson ranging from 0.826 to 0.967 (all <.001) and Spearman ρ ranging from 0.866 to 0.991. Informal qualitative comments frequently described the outputs as linguistically organized and clinically interpretable, while also noting limited affective variability and contextual integration. Conclusions: The findings suggest that LLMs can reproduce the formal linguistic structure of reflective discourse, generating outputs perceived by clinicians as coherent and clinically interpretable across multiple dimensions of mentalization. However, within the present evaluative framework, this performance appears more consistent with structural language regularities than with evidence of experiential, affective, or intentional processes. These results support using LLMs as research and training tools for studying the linguistic aspects of mentalization, while highlighting the continuing importance of human clinical judgment in contexts requiring emotional, relational, and contextual integration.
title: Algorithmic Reflectivity in Large Language Models: Methodological Study of Linguistic Structure in Mentalization

summary: Background: Patients with cancer frequently experience complex and multidimensional symptom burdens. Standardized patient-reported outcome measures provide structured approaches to symptom assessment but may not capture the full range of symptom-related and psychosocial concerns expressed in patients’ narratives. Patient-generated social media data offer a complementary source for examining how these concerns are expressed online. Objective: This study aimed to characterize cancer symptom–related narratives in Chinese social media posts using a conventional symptom assessment framework and to identify additional experiential themes through neural topic modeling. Methods: A computational text analysis integrating large language model (LLM) annotation and neural topic modeling was conducted. A corpus of 26,086 first-person patient narratives was collected from Xiaohongshu and Zhihu between November 2013 and February 2026 using cancer-related search terms. First-person narratives and 6 SPPADE (sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and low energy or fatigue) symptom domains were identified using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI) and validated against independent human coding. Symptom occurrence, co-occurrence, multiplicity, and coping strategies were characterized, with exploratory stratified analyses by cancer type. BERTopic modeling was applied to identify latent themes, platform sensitivity analyses, and temporal distribution were examined. Results: For first-person narrative identification, human raters showed 89.2% agreement (Cohen κ=0.784); the LLM achieved an -score of 81.2% against the adjudicated reference standard. For SPPADE extraction, mean Cohen κ values for LLM-human agreement were 0.714 (SD 0.114) and 0.754 (SD 0.095) across the 6 symptom domains. Overall, 13,896 of 26,086 (53.3%) posts contained at least 1 identifiable symptom. Pain was the most frequently identified symptom (5783/26,086, 22.2%), followed by physical function impairment (4153/26,086, 15.9%) and depression (4050/26,086, 15.5%). Pain and physical function impairment formed the most frequent co-occurring symptom pair (n=1407). Coping strategies were described in 7104/26,086 (27.2%) posts; medication-based approaches were most prominent, particularly for pain and sleep disturbance, while social and psychological support were more common for anxiety and depression. BERTopic modeling identified 13 latent themes, including cancer treatment trajectories, health care system interaction, existential distress, family involvement, and financial burden, highlighting experiential concerns that may be underrepresented in conventional symptom assessment. The proportion of posts containing at least 1 SPPADE symptom was similar between Xiaohongshu and Zhihu (53.2% vs 54.1%; =.35), although individual symptom distributions differed across platforms. Conclusions: Chinese social media posts contained multidimensional symptom-related narratives alongside psychosocial and experiential concerns that may be less visible in structured symptom assessment. Patient-generated social media data may therefore provide a complementary source for understanding cancer symptom experiences and supportive care concerns. However, differences in platform composition, uneven temporal coverage, and the nonrepresentativeness of social media users limit generalizability, and the clinical utility of integrating such data into routine symptom assessment requires further evaluation.
title: Characterizing Cancer Symptom Experiences and Related Psychosocial Concerns Through Chinese Social Media Narratives: Computational Text Analysis

summary:
Objective

To evaluate whether providing authors with a manuscript template structured according to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) 2025 reporting guideline for use during revision improves the completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols.

Design

Randomised controlled trial.

Setting

BMJ Open.

Population

70 of 74 manuscripts screened between 29 April and 27 May 2025 that reported randomised controlled trial protocols with a decision of minor or major revision after the first round of peer review were randomly allocated (1:1) using an R generated sequence. Authors were not informed of the study.

Interventions

Handling editors asked the intervention group authors to use a SPIRIT based manuscript template when preparing their first revision. The template included structured subheadings corresponding to SPIRIT 2025 items, along with guidance on reporting. Editorial decisions were not conditional on use of the template. Control group manuscripts underwent standard peer review.

Main outcome measures

The primary outcome was completeness of reporting score in the revised manuscript (adjusted for baseline), calculated as the mean of 11 SPIRIT items that are frequently inadequately reported (each scored 0, 0.5, or 1) and linearly rescaled to a 0-10 score. After submission of their first revision, authors in the intervention group completed an online survey. The survey included both fixed response and open ended questions designed to capture the authors' perceptions of ease of use, helpfulness, and any challenges encountered when using the template. Secondary outcomes included mean completeness of reporting scores for each item, median time to submission of the revised manuscript, and authors' experiences of using the template. Outcome assessors, but not editors or investigators, were masked.

Results

Of the 70 manuscripts randomised (35 in each group), all were analysed, with no loss to follow-up. In the intervention group, completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols improved by 0.61 points (95% confidence interval 0.20 to 1.01) compared with the control group, with mean (standard deviation) scores increasing from 5.42 (1.07) to 6.70 (1.23) and 5.77 (1.19) to 6.32 (0.94), respectively. The largest improvements were observed for recruitment, data collection methods, and access to data. Median time to submission of the first revision was similar between the intervention and control groups (27.10 v 29.86 days, respectively). Data on harms were not systematically collected. Among 14 of 35 survey respondents (40%), many (8/13, 62%) reported the template as time consuming and some (5/13, 39%) as burdensome. Most respondents, however, found it easy to use (10/13, 77%), helpful for improving the manuscript (9/13, 69%), and reassuring for adherence to SPIRIT (13/13, 100%).

Conclusions

Providing authors of randomised controlled trials with a SPIRIT based template during manuscript revision modestly improved the completeness of reporting in the trial protocols without extending revision times.

Trial registration

Open Science Framework 10.17605/OSF.IO/C4YQZ.
title: Effectiveness of a structured template to improve completeness of reporting randomised trial protocols: randomised controlled trial.

summary: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.
title: Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior in human–AI collaborative diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum

summary: Background: Clinical practice guidelines are central instruments of evidence-based care; yet, in many domains, particularly rare or complex diseases, multiple guidelines coexist and frequently offer conflicting advice. Existing strategies for resolving such divergences are often labor-intensive, opaque, and insufficiently reproducible. Objective: This tutorial aimed to develop and demonstrate a reproducible workflow for transforming divergent clinical guideline recommendations and literature-derived white areas into human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items. Methods: Following a step-by-step tutorial structure, we demonstrate the workflow using penile cancer as a worked example. The process comprises manual selection of clinical guidelines, a systematic PubMed search for literature-derived candidate issues potentially unaddressed by the selected guidelines, selection of 3 complementary large language models (LLMs), and execution of predefined prompts, multimodal recommendation extraction, semantic harmonization, and item-level guideline stance classification. The evaluative process combines a 3-LLM ensemble consistency check with an independent pre-Delphi appraisal by 4 penile cancer experts using a predefined 5-point suitability scale and acceptance threshold. Results: In the worked example in the field of penile cancer as a high-stakes use case, the workflow extracted 157 clinical recommendations from 5 guidelines and consolidated them into 68 harmonized guideline-derived items. Stance classification identified 15 uniformly supported items and 53 divergent, ambiguous, or incompletely addressed items. In parallel, literature processing generated 95 harmonized white-area items, of which 9 were classified as true white-area items not addressed by the included guidelines. The final methodological output was a set of 62 human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items for subsequent clinical consensus voting. Conclusions: This methodology provides a scalable, transparent, and transferable approach for identifying and structuring interguideline inconsistencies and evidence gaps. By combining LLM-assisted analysis with independent external expert appraisal, it supports the reproducible transformation of heterogeneous guideline content into Delphi-ready candidate items.
title: From Divergent Guidelines to Delphi-Ready Items: Tutorial for Large Language Model–Assisted Guideline Harmonization Using Penile Cancer as a Worked Example

summary: Background: Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques. Objective: The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes. Results: Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI −0.011 to 0.033 units per day; =.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; =.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=−0.214, 95% CI −0.255 to −0.172 vs control group point estimate=−0.122, 95% CI −0.163 to −0.081; =.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; =.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods. Conclusions: DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06026280; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06026280 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/62715
title: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: The use of medical real-world data is constrained by fragmented data infrastructures and the absence of tools integrating longitudinal clinical with molecular data at scale. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common monogenic cause of kidney failure, exemplifies this gap given its phenotypic complexity and the need for individualized treatment decisions. We present MEDA-PKD (MEdical DAta translation service of Polycystic Kidney Disease), an interactive, near-real-time analytics platform that integrates clinical routine with research data from the German AD(H)PKD Tolvaptan Registry (NCT02497521, DRKS00008910) into a harmonized database ( https://doi.org/10.18716/adpkd_registry ). MEDA-PKD provides automated near-real-time analysis and dynamic visualization, replacing traditional static approaches to clinical cohorts. As of March 2026, MEDA-PKD visualized data from 1735 patients (mean follow-up 796 days). eGFR slope analysis of data from patients initiating tolvaptan therapy (332 patients) demonstrates the platform’s capacity to evaluate real-world therapeutic impact in real-time. Other tabs include family history, medication, lifestyle, quality of life and a wide array of lab values (20,894 entries). Besides, MEDA-PKD integrates proteomics data and allows for secure individual patient-level data access. MEDA-PKD represents a paradigm shift by transforming static cohort data into a living, actionable knowledge resource in ADPKD and will serve as a template for other diseases.
title: MEDA-PKD: a dynamic, real-time analytics platform for precision care in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

summary: Background: AI-based tools for oral cancer screening have shown promising performance in curated image datasets, but their performance in real-world mobile community screening workflows remains less clear. Objective: This study evaluated the prospective field performance of a parameter-locked, mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system embedded in a human-supervised community oral cancer screening workflow. Methods: We conducted a prospective community-based field evaluation in eastern Taiwan from June 17 to December 31, 2025. Trained nonspecialist personnel acquired standard white-light intraoral images using handheld mobile devices during routine screening. The AI system incorporated on-site image quality assessment and lesion-level risk stratification into green, yellow, and red triage categories. Technically inadequate images after repeated acquisition attempts were classified as ungradable and excluded from performance analysis. Three board-certified oral and maxillofacial specialists established an operational clinical reference standard through structured image review and consensus adjudication. The primary outcome was lesion-level identification of high-risk lesions requiring specialist referral, defined as red versus nonred triage. Diagnostic performance was estimated with Wilson 95% CIs; precision-recall performance and preconsensus specialist agreement were also assessed. Results: Among 602 screened participants, 4283 interpretable intraoral images were included in expert adjudication and lesion-level analysis. The AI system flagged 68 red lesions; 12 (17.6%) were confirmed as high risk, and 4 additional high-risk lesions were identified during expert review, yielding 16 high-risk events for the primary red-triage analysis. For high-risk lesion identification, sensitivity was 75% (12/16; 95% CI 50.5%-89.8%) and positive predictive value was 17.6% (12/68; 95% CI 10.4%-28.4%); specificity, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 98.6% (3928/3984), 99.9% (3928/3932), and 98.5% (3940/4000), respectively. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values were 0.957 for red, 0.931 for yellow, and 0.964 for green triage; precision-recall analysis showed area under the precision-recall curve values of 0.8235, 0.9052, and 0.9476, respectively. Preconsensus specialist agreement was high, with a Fleiss κ of 0.921 and a Gwet AC1 of 0.981. Conclusions: This mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system was feasibly integrated into a real-world community screening workflow operated by trained nonspecialist personnel. In this low-prevalence field setting, red triage showed moderate sensitivity and modest positive predictive value, supporting its use as human-supervised referral-prioritization support rather than autonomous diagnosis. Further multicenter studies with blinded assessment, participant-level outcomes, workflow-efficiency measures, and longitudinal follow-up are needed before clinical impact and scalability can be determined.
title: Mobile AI-Assisted Oral Lesion Triage for Community Oral Cancer Screening: Prospective Field Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Engagement with suicide-related content online is often assumed to be harmful, yet many individuals with lived experience describe such content as supportive or even life-preserving. Despite policy and clinical concerns, little is known about how people intentionally or unintentionally encounter this content, how they interpret it, and how these experiences shape perceived harm or benefit. Objective: This study aims to explore how intent and context influence the ways in which individuals with lived experience of suicidality encounter, interpret, and respond to suicide-related online content, and to identify factors associated with perceived harm and benefit. Methods: An exploratory cross-sectional survey was conducted with a convenience sample of 713 UK-based participants aged 16 to 60 years and older, 95.9% (n=684) of whom reported having lived experience of suicidality. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-square tests, to examine associations between engagement patterns, intent, and suicidality. Free-text responses were coded using content analysis to identify categories relating to motivations for engagement, emotional responses, and perceived impact. Results: Participants reported a broad range of experiences. While 30.0% (214/713) described suicide-related content as contributing to suicidal thoughts or attempts, others reported relief, validation, or reduced feelings of isolation, with 21.0% (150/713) attributing content to preventing an attempt. Clear differences emerged between participants who actively sought out content (“seekers”) and those who encountered it unintentionally (“stumblers”). Seekers more frequently reported positive or understanding responses, often in the context of unmet offline support needs, whereas stumblers were more likely to report shock or distress. Approximately 39.9% (151/378) of participants described their engagement as neither intentional nor accidental, potentially reflecting a blurred boundary between passive exposure and active seeking, as well as the difficulty individuals face in accurately identifying and articulating their own motivations in relation to suicidality. Conclusions: Engagement with suicide-related online content cannot be characterized as uniformly harmful. Outcomes depend on user intent, emotional state, and the context of engagement, and they may change over time. Clinical, regulatory, and policy approaches should move beyond risk-only frameworks to account for the nuanced and sometimes supportive roles such content plays in how individuals make sense of suicidal thoughts, while still protecting those at risk.
title: Navigating Suicide-Related Online Content in Individuals With Lived Experience of Suicidality: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary:
Background

The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs).

Objective

To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations.

Design

Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective.

Setting

Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026.

Participants

No human participants were involved.

Measurements

Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action).

Results

The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%).

Limitations

Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.

Conclusion

The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.

Primary funding source

None.
title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Patient access to their electronic health records (EHRs) could improve care and reduce errors by enabling patient contribution to documentation. However, interactive functions that support such engagement remain underresearched. <strong>Objective:</strong> The purpose of this study was to analyze patients’ use of the free-text comment function in the Swedish national patient-accessible EHR. <strong>Methods:</strong> Comments made by patients between 2015 and 2021 for health care professionals to view were retrieved from the patient-accessible EHR administration service in Sweden. The number and length of comments were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests, while the content was examined qualitatively using inductive content analysis. In addition, comments were coded for sentiment (positive, neutral, or negative) and note content, and users were classified according to whether they had submitted at least 1 comment referring to mental health care. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 1670 comments were left by 659 patients, of which 15 had irrelevant content (15/1670, 0.9%; 95% CI 0.4%-1.4%), leaving 1655 comments for analysis. Most comments (948/1655, 57.3%; 95% CI 54.9%-59.7%) were related to matters other than note content, and nearly all had a neutral (920/1655, 55.6%; 95% CI 53.2%-58.0%) or negative (702/1655, 42.4%; 95% CI 40.0%-44.8%) sentiment. Patients who submitted a comment referencing mental health care tended to leave more comments overall (median 7 vs 2 comments per patient), and their comments were more frequently negative than comments written by other patients (313/495, 63.2% vs 389/1160, 33.5%; <i>P</i><.001). The most prevalent categories were care engagement, perceived inaccuracies, complaints, and requests. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Patient engagement with clinical notes has the potential to enhance documentation accuracy and strengthen patient-clinician communication. To realize these benefits safely, such features must be deliberately designed and clearly explained to users to avoid patient safety risks and unnecessary burdens on health care professionals.
title: Patient Use of a Comment Function in Electronic Health Records: Mixed Methods Case Study

summary: Lung puncture biopsy is the gold standard for the qualitative diagnosis of lung nodules. Cone Beam CT (CBCT) is commonly used for guiding punctures to locate lung nodules. However, the poor quality of CBCT images and the limited intelligence of surgical guidance systems have lowered the efficiency of puncture procedures, particularly for small and complex lesions. This study developed and validated a robust and accurate Generative AI-Powered Puncture Surgery Navigation System for lung punctures (GPS-Lung), demonstrating clinical applicability through a multicenter randomized controlled trial (Registration number: NCT06762613). The clinical results showed significant improvements in surgeon performance with the assistance of the integrated GPS-Lung system. Specifically, the system facilitated a more standardized and efficient operational process, reducing number of punctures (2.0 ± 1.2 vs. 2.5 ± 1.7, P = 0.005), shortening operative time (20.4 ± 5.6 min vs. 23.2 ± 6.3 min, P = 0.001), decreasing radiation exposure (4357.4 ± 3427.3 μGy·m2 vs. 5570.9 ± 4846.7 μGy·m2, P = 0.033), and reducing pneumothorax complications (12.7% vs. 23.9%, P = 0.033). Taken together, the proposed system demonstrates promising clinical and translational value in lung nodule puncture intervention. (Clinical Trials Registration: NCT06762613). Clinical Trials Registration: NCT06762613, Registration Date: March 26, 2025. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06762613?term=NCT06762613&rank=1&tab=history).
title: A Generative AI-powered navigation system for precision CBCT-guided lung biopsies: a randomized controlled trial

summary: Background: The rise of online mental health communities has reshaped the ways individuals seek and receive mental health support. Although online mental health communities (OMHCs) offer a valuable space for peer support, including through experience-sharing, they also present challenges, including moderation practices to cultivate supportive interactions and secure member safety. No comprehensive framework of moderation practices has been established. Developing such an understanding is important, as moderators play a central role in facilitating a sense of community and determining whether OMHCs function as safe and supportive spaces. Objective: This study aimed to develop typologies of moderator practices used to support safety and facilitate a sense of community within OMHCs for people with mental health problems, and the content of OMHC community guidelines. Methods: A systematized review of empirical research studies focusing on moderation practices and community guidelines in OMHCs was conducted using MEDLINE, Web of Science, Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, supplemented with a purposive search to identify gray literature on community guidelines for OMHC moderation. Inclusion criteria: online, text-based component, asynchronous or synchronous moderation, mental health–related focus, and human moderation. Exclusion criteria: crisis-focused, audience-based, nonmoderated or bot-moderated, profession not peer support, non-English, and academic review or thesis. The search period was 2014 to 2024. A bespoke data extraction sheet was piloted, then populated, capturing document, OMHC, member, and moderator characteristics. Thematic analysis was used to synthesize the findings relating to each objective. Results: The systematized search identified 11,347 studies and other documents, from which 80 studies were included, comprising 48 empirical papers and 32 gray literature documents. These related to 52 different OMHCs. Four categories of moderator practices were identified: (1) premoderation and postmoderation processes, (2) reactive moderation processes, (3) building the community, and (4) monitoring members. Premoderation and postmoderation processes were used within 41 (79%) of the 52 OMHCs. Three categories of community guideline content were identified: (1) content of post, (2) member conduct, and (3) moderation. The category, content of post, was the most widely used component of community guidelines, used in 35 (67%) of the 52 OMHCs. Conclusions: The two typologies provide a foundational framework that can be adapted and applied to community guidelines and moderation strategies across a range of contexts. When operationalized, they could provide benefit to people with mental health problems by using them to guide the development of moderator training, digital tools, and governance policies that align with the specific characteristics and objectives of individual OMHCs. Effective translation and application of these typologies require careful, nuanced consideration of each community’s goals, membership, and cultural context to ensure their relevance, effectiveness, and impact.
title: A Typology of Moderator Practices and Community Guidelines in Online Mental Health Communities to Establish a Framework for Digital Safety: Systematized Review

summary: Background: Health AI investment is accelerating across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), yet the region’s health AI research output has never been systematically quantified. National research capacity is a structural precondition for the safe local development and governance of clinical AI, but no scientometric baseline exists for the 6 GCC states. Objective: We characterized the volume, growth, collaboration structure, and thematic composition of GCC health AI research and examined whether national output aligns with an existing measure of informatics readiness. Methods: We conducted an ecological scientometric analysis of all health AI publications affiliated with the 6 GCC states (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates) for 2011 to 2024 (the last complete indexing year at extraction) using the open bibliographic database OpenAlex. A publication was eligible if it included both an AI family and a health or medicine family concept above a 0.30 relevance threshold. Bibliometric indicators (output, compound annual growth, per capita intensity, citation impact, international and intraregional collaboration, and institutional concentration) were computed; coauthorship and concept co-occurrence networks were constructed and clustered by modularity. National health AI intensity was correlated (Spearman) with the Health Informatics Readiness Index (HIRI) and Global Digital Health Monitor (GDHM) phase. Results: Of 112,480 GCC-affiliated AI publications, 3512 met the health AI definition. Regional output rose from 18 (2011) to 904 (2024) publications per year (compound annual growth=35.2%), with 86.4% (3034/3512) published from 2020 onward and a sharp inflection from 2019 to 2021. Saudi Arabia contributed 59.6% (2094/3512) of the output by itself and 81.5% (2862/3512) together with the United Arab Emirates; Qatar led on a per capita basis (approximately 136 publications per million population). International collaboration (2551/3512, 72.6% of the papers) predominated over intra-GCC collaboration (164/3327, 4.9%), with the latter being inversely related to national output. The principal external partners were India, the United States, Pakistan, the United Kingdom, and Egypt. Output spanned 3186 institutions; concentration ranged from 89.4% (328/367) of a country’s output among the top 3 institutions for Qatar to 34.4% (721/2094) for Saudi Arabia. Concept co-occurrence was classified into 4 themes—classic machine learning clinical prediction, medical imaging and oncology, COVID-19 response, and diabetic eye disease. Health AI intensity (ρ=+0.60) and, more strongly, absolute output (ρ=+0.89) correlated with the HIRI; absolute output was also correlated with GDHM phase (ρ=+0.83). Conclusions: GCC health AI research has grown rapidly but unevenly, is heavily dependent on international collaboration, is concentrated in medical imaging, and—outside Saudi Arabia—remains anchored in single national institutions. Informatics readiness was associated with both the intensity and the volume of national research output. The findings establish a reproducible baseline for monitoring regional health AI research capacity as GCC health systems move toward clinical AI deployment.
title: Capacity, Collaboration, and Thematic Structure in Health AI Research Over the Past Decade in the Gulf Cooperation Council: Scientometric Analysis

summary: Background: Smart care robots are increasingly viewed as a potential way to address care burden and support care quality in long-term care facilities. However, their integration into routine care practice remains limited, and the conditions required for their effective implementation are not yet well understood from the perspective of frontline nursing assistants. Objective: This study aimed to clarify nursing assistants’ core functional expectations of smart care robots in long-term care facilities and to explore the key conditions for their integration into practice. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted. Using purposive sampling, 31 frontline nursing assistants were recruited from 5 long-term care facilities in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, with recruitment assistance from facility administrators and eligibility screening by the research team. Semistructured face-to-face interviews were conducted between September and November 2025. Data were analyzed using framework analysis. Results: Framework analysis produced 4 analytical domains: real-world care needs, limited facilitating conditions, major anticipated barriers, and preparatory pathways for implementation. Participants expected robots to support safety monitoring and risk warning, standardized checking and management, repetitive physical tasks, and basic interaction. Although some openness to technology and organizational support existed, these facilitating conditions were insufficient for routine implementation. Key barriers included unclear human-robot collaboration models, inadequate organizational capacity, potential new care risks, and weak external support. Participants emphasized organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, pilot testing, and structured training as essential preparatory steps. Emotional support functions were also valued for alleviating caregivers’ emotional burden in high-intensity care work. Conclusions: Openness to technology, supportive organizational climates, and positive policy and social signals provided an initial foundation for considering robot integration. However, uncertainties remained around human-robot collaboration, risk management, organizational capacity, and concrete external support. Organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, real-world pilot testing, and practical training warrant further evaluation before wider implementation.
title: Conditions and Pathways for Integrating Smart Care Robots Into Long-Term Care Facilities: Qualitative Study From Nursing Assistants’ Perspectives

summary: Background: Cross-domain chest radiograph report generation may produce formally valid reports that are nevertheless repetitive, weakly case-specific, or missing clinically relevant findings. These failures can be missed when evaluation relies on a single language-overlap or clinical-label score. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate cross-domain report generation with a bidirectional layered audit, characterize direction-specific and end point–specific failure profiles under a composite training-side control and 3 decoding policies, and explore whether selected audit dimensions remained informative for a contemporary medical vision language model. Methods: A fixed R2Gen-style system was evaluated bidirectionally on 575 IU X-ray and 401 MIMIC-CXR (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care Chest X-Ray) target records. The audit included surface validity, complete-report recurrence and concentration, a predefined prefix end point, lexical diversity, official Stanford CheXpert/NegBio labels, paired cluster-bootstrap inference, and blinded review by 2 medical trainees. The primary human audit included 210 reports from 70 randomly sampled cases, with blinded adjudication of unresolved primary end point disagreements. A 60-report targeted panel was used for failure-mode analysis. Separately, a fixed MedGemma 1.5 4B configuration generated reports for all 976 records. Results: In MIMIC-CXR–to–IU X-ray transfer, out of 575 reports, ON (protocol-defined training-side control enabled)+B4 (beam search with a beam size of 4) reduced the predefined recurrent prefix from 575 (100%) to 8 (1.4%; Holm-adjusted =.002). However, 569 (99.0%) ON+B4 outputs still belonged to exact duplicate groups. In IU X-ray–to–MIMIC-CXR transfer, the 14-category CheXpert/NegBio micro- was higher for ON+B4 than for OFF (protocol-defined training-side control disabled)+B4 (0.1687 vs 0.0744; Holm-adjusted =.01). This apparent advantage was not broad-based: after cardiomegaly was excluded in a post hoc descriptive sensitivity analysis, the difference changed from +0.0944 to −0.0610. Text-level tracing showed that the original contrast was mainly driven by a labeler response to recurrent, semantically normal heart-size wording. Across the primary human-audit cells, major omissions occurred in 12 to 15 out of 35 reports, and major unsupported findings occurred in 10 to 16 of 35 reports, with no consistent configuration ordering observed. The exploratory MedGemma micro- was 0.4722 on IU X-ray and 0.4340 on MIMIC-CXR, but 381 out of 575 (66.3%) IU outputs belonged to exact duplicate groups. Conclusions: No configuration performed consistently well across end points, and no single metric captured all forms of cross-domain degradation. The MedGemma stress test suggested that recurrence and label-traceability checks remain useful across architectures, although it was not a matched performance comparison. Cross-domain report generators should undergo bidirectional evaluation, final-text verification, and image-grounded human review before external validation or clinical deployment.
title: Cross-Domain Chest Radiograph Report Generation Under Dataset Shift: Bidirectional Audit Study

summary: Background: Globally, the carbon footprint of the health care sector is significant and growing, and digital health care technologies (DHTs) offer unique opportunities to reduce the carbon footprint of health and care systems. However, their environmental impact has not been adequately investigated. Objective: This scoping review aims to explore the environmental impact of DHTs, focusing on reducing their carbon footprint and evaluating methods for assessing that impact. Methods: This scoping review followed the method outlined by Arksey and O’Malley, adhering to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. The databases of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published in English with no time limitation. Search terms were categorized under three broader concepts: “Digital Health Technologies,” “Health and Care,” and “Carbon Footprint.” Studies were included based on screening titles and abstracts, followed by review of full-text papers by at least 2 reviewers. Narrative synthesis was used to report the findings. Results: The database search yielded 4274 studies. Following screening and reference list checks, 70 studies were selected for inclusion. The earliest included study was published in 2007, with the majority originating from the United States (n=26) and the United Kingdom (n=12). Most studies assessed telemedicine or telehealth interventions. Retrospective analyses predominated, although prospective, cross-sectional, mixed method, and life cycle assessment (LCA) designs were also reported. Environmental impact was most often evaluated through travel-related carbon savings, with some studies incorporating energy use, medical equipment or resources, infrastructure, or waste. LCA studies applied process-based approaches that included detailed activity- and product-specific data, as well as Environmentally Extended Input-Output (EEIO) models. In most cases, carbon footprint measurements were based on assumptions, with calculations relying on published emission factors or calculators. Some studies have expressed CO emissions using emission equivalencies, such as equivalent carbon sequestration and equivalent CO emissions. Overall, DHTs demonstrated positive environmental impacts by reducing carbon footprint. However, negative impacts, especially electricity consumption and the lifecycle impacts of digital devices, were also noted. Conclusions: DHTs are associated with reductions in carbon emissions and related environmental benefits, with telemedicine showing potential to lower the carbon footprint of the health care sector. However, evidence highlights the negative impacts associated with energy demand and the full lifecycle of digital devices. Given the substantial heterogeneity in assessment methods and outcome measures across studies, these findings should be interpreted with caution. To capture the true environmental implications of digital health, more rigorous, standardized, and comprehensive assessment methods are required. Bridging these methodological gaps is essential to ensure that DHTs not only support sustainable health care delivery but also make a meaningful contribution to mitigating global climate change. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/gdnve; https://osf.io/gdnve/overview
title: Environmental Impact of Digital Health Care Technologies in Reducing Carbon Footprints: Scoping Review

summary: Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable burden among children, particularly in low-income settings. Despite decades of progress, there are indications of measles resurgence due to stagnation in vaccine coverage. Here, using the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we systematically assessed measles incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and vaccine coverage (measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1) and measles-containing vaccine 2 (MCV2)) among children under 5 years of age across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Between 1990 and 2019, global measles incidence and mortality declined by approximately 80% and 90%, respectively, but rebounded sharply after 2020, with 15.6 million cases and 118,000 deaths estimated in 2023 (+40% and +12% increases, respectively, between 2019 and 2023). Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia continue to bear the highest burden. Global MCV1 coverage rose from 67.2% in 1990 to 83.6% in 2019 but stalled and declined slightly to 81.0% by 2023; MCV2 coverage increased from 14.4% in 1990 to 68.4% in 2019 and reached 71.4% by 2023. Several regions remain well below the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) target of 90% coverage. The recent measles resurgence underscores the fragility of global immunization progress and the urgent need to restore routine vaccination, close immunity gaps and strengthen outbreak preparedness. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease Study showed that although global measles incidence and mortality had declined in 1990−2019, its resurgence since 2020 reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.
