summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) are central to patient-centered care. However, many current EHR systems do not represent, exchange, or reuse genomic findings in structured, interoperable, and clinically actionable forms. Instead, genomic results are often retained in static reports. This limits their use in routine clinical care and clinical decision support. It also restricts their future reinterpretation as scientific knowledge evolves, as well as their reuse for research within appropriate governance frameworks. To support precision and personalized medicine, we advocate that clinically relevant genomic findings should be represented within EHRs as structured, phenotype-linked, interoperable, and versioned data. Raw and intermediate genomic files, however, should remain in appropriately governed laboratory or genomics repositories. This viewpoint is intended for health policymakers, health informatics leaders, EHR developers, research and clinical genomics laboratories, and clinicians involved in implementing genomics into routine care. It is informed by selected published literature and relevant technical standards. It is also informed by operational experience at the Cyprus Institute of Neurology and Genetics and multidisciplinary discussions from the Gen2EHR Implementation Guidelines Workshop conducted within the Extended EHR@EU Data Space and European Health Data Space for Secondary Use @CY initiatives. We examine technical, organizational, clinical, ethical, legal, and governance challenges, including inconsistent reporting formats and unclear clinical responsibility. We propose a staged, workshop-informed implementation pathway for evaluation within the European Health Data Space. The pathway combines Health Level 7 Fast Health Interoperability Resources Genomics Reporting with complementary standards and terminologies. It also includes transitional dual PDF and structured Fast Health Interoperability Resources reporting, governance for access, version control, reinterpretation, and clinical responsibility, as well as multidisciplinary pilot validation in real diagnostic workflows. The clinical effectiveness and transferability of the proposed pathway across European health systems remain to be established.
title: Making Genomic Data Actionable in Electronic Health Records: Practical Viewpoint on Standards, Governance, and Implementation

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Depression is heterogeneous and dynamic, and changes in observable behavior may accompany some of its clinical manifestations. Digital devices offer new opportunities to capture this behavior in naturalistic settings continuously. However, the specific digital features captured through device interactions and their relationships to depression-related outcomes have yet to be synthesized, and their potential relevance to functional constructs is unclear. The research domain criteria (RDoC) may provide a conceptual framework for exploring potential links between digital behaviors and functional constructs. <strong>Objective:</strong> This scoping review aimed (1) to identify and summarize key online behavioral modalities and their specific features for depression monitoring and assessment, (2) to summarize existing evidence on associations between specific behavioral features and depression-related outcomes, and (3) to explore whether the behavioral content captured by digital measures has the potential conceptual links to RDoC constructs. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a scoping review of 5 databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PsycINFO) from inception through January 2026, supplemented by citation tracking and gray literature searches. Included studies focused on online behavioral digital phenotyping for depression and reported specific behavioral features. Two reviewers (QR and JC) independently screened studies and extracted data, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (YH). Findings were synthesized descriptively. Two reviewers (QR and Kaili Tang) independently assessed potential conceptual links between each behavioral modality and RDoC constructs using the official RDoC construct definitions. <strong>Results:</strong> In total, 74 studies were included. Five primary behavioral modalities were identified: call behavior (n=31), SMS (n=21), screen use (n=41), app use (n=26), and keystroke dynamics (n=14), comprising 36 core features. A total of 31 (41.9%) studies reported findings attributable to individual features, but no single feature showed a consistently directed association with depression-related outcomes across studies. An exploratory RDoC assessment suggested that candidate construct relevance primarily involved social processes, sensorimotor systems, cognitive systems, and arousal and regulatory systems. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Online behavioral digital phenotyping captures a range of observable behaviors, but current evidence does not support interpreting individual digital behavioral features as stable markers of depression or as direct proxies for specific RDoC constructs. Future research should improve the transparency of feature definitions and reporting, strengthen the reporting of feature-level findings, and use independent validation and construct-informed study designs to enhance interpretability.
title: Online Behavioral Digital Phenotyping for Depression: Scoping Review of Behavioral Features and Exploratory Assessment of Research Domain Criteria Construct Relevance

summary: Background: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) aims to optimize clinical outcomes but is hindered by logistical delays and susceptibility to data errors. Integrating model-informed precision dosing with point-of-care testing, fortified by rule-based validation and alerts, forms a transformative clinical decision support system (CDSS) essential for securing this complex workflow. Objective: This study evaluates, , the effectiveness of a rule-based CDSS for imatinib in detecting data-quality issues and optimizing therapeutic dosing, compared with a human TDM expert. Methods: We simulated a set of 60 virtual patients using a previously developed population pharmacokinetic model and deliberately enriched it with data-quality errors (eg, timing inaccuracies and reporting errors) to stress-test system resilience. summary: Background: The development of structured optical character recognition (OCR) systems for Korean medical documents is hindered by strict privacy regulations that limit access to real clinical data. Existing synthetic document frameworks are primarily designed for generic layouts and Western languages, and fail to capture the complex formatting, bilingual terminology, and hierarchical field semantics required for clinical OCR and document-understanding tasks in hospital environments. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a privacy-preserving, template-driven pipeline for generating realistic synthetic Korean medical documents with structured XML annotations, enabling OCR and document-understanding model training in settings where access to real clinical data is restricted. Methods: We designed MedDocSynth, a 7-stage synthetic document generation pipeline that reconstructs authentic medical document layouts from publicly available references, incorporates clinician-guided template selection, and uses a structured placeholder system encoding 17 medical data types. Human-curated templates were populated with exemplar content and tagged using a delimiter-based scheme, after which GPT-4o-mini generated diverse synthetic values for each field. The pipeline produced 1000 fully synthetic DOCX documents with corresponding XML annotations encoding hierarchical structure, title-answer relationships, and datatype metadata. We evaluated text fidelity, lexical diversity (type-token ratio, measure of textual lexical diversity [MTLD], n-grams, and Pareto), and compared the system with existing synthetic document pipelines. A Qwen2.5-VL model was fine-tuned exclusively on the synthetic dataset and evaluated on 50 real-world Korean clinical documents to assess OCR accuracy, information extraction, and table reconstruction. Results: The pipeline achieved 100% placeholder coverage, 99.68% format correctness, and 91.56% semantic accuracy. Lexical diversity analysis demonstrated high variability in free-text fields (MTLD≈456) and expected repetitiveness in structured datatypes. Compared with existing pipelines (SynthText, SynthTiger, and DocSynth), the proposed system uniquely supports complex clinical forms, bilingual content, and structured XML annotations. When trained solely on the synthetic data, Qwen2.5-VL achieved the highest real-world performance, with a character accuracy of 86.01%, word accuracy of 78.25%, field accuracy of 67.18%, datatype accuracy of 64.14%, and table reconstruction tree-edit-distance similarity score of 71.09%. Models without fine-tuning performed substantially worse, including GPT-5-mini. Conclusions: We present the first synthetic data generation pipeline specifically tailored to Korean medical documents, enabling the creation of realistic, richly annotated datasets for structured OCR without exposing patient information. The synthetic data significantly improves OCR performance on real clinical documents, demonstrating the pipeline’s potential utility for hospital deployment and its potential extensibility to other languages and health care systems.
title: Synthetic Medical Document Generation Pipeline (MedDocSynth) for Optical Character Recognition: Development and Validation Study on Korean Clinical Documents

summary: Background: Use of secure messaging within the patient portal has grown rapidly over recent years, yet clinical workflows, staffing models, and billing practices have generally not been comprehensively adapted to support this increasing volume of messages. Little is known about the characteristics of patients who are high-volume message senders, and we lack a nuanced understanding of patient messaging intensity beyond measures accounting for sheer volume, limiting health system efforts to anticipate message-related workflow demands and allocate resources effectively. Objective: Our objective was to characterize older adult patients (aged ≥65 years) with high secure messaging volume, examining both patient characteristics and other aspects of their messaging intensity, such as messaging frequency, length, and messaging use relative to patient portal logins and health care encounters. Methods: We analyzed electronic medical record and patient portal data from a large academic health system, encompassing 16,023 older adults who sent 199,981 messages over a 12-month period. We developed 5 measures to account for secure messaging intensity. Our primary measure of messaging intensity was based on message volume; high-volume message senders were identified using outlier analysis based on patients’ aggregate number of messages sent during the observation period. Additional measures of messaging intensity included identifying individuals with concentrated periods of messaging, message length (character count), a ratio of messages to portal logins, and a ratio of messages to health care encounters. We compared sociodemographic characteristics, health status, and messaging intensity of high-volume secure messaging senders with those of other message senders. Results: Of 16,023 older adult patients who sent at least 1 message during the observation period, 1298 (8.1%) were classified as high-volume message senders; these patients accounted for 39.7% (79,475/199,981) of total messages. High-volume message senders, compared with all other message senders, were more likely to be White (1044/1298, 80.4% vs 10,670/14,725, 72.5%; <.001), have higher comorbidity scores (2.6 vs 1.8; <.001), and higher incidence of cancer (465/1298, 35.8% vs 3354/14,725, 22.8%; <.001) and dementia (107/1298, 8.2% vs 889/14,725, 6.1%; <.002). High-volume message senders were also more likely to be identified as having concentrated periods of messaging, to send longer messages, and to send more messages in relation to patient portal logins and health care encounters. Conclusions: High-volume message senders represent a small but distinct group of older patients who send a large share of messages to clinicians. Using multiple measures of messaging intensity can provide additional context about patient messaging behavior and help health systems redesign workflows and care delivery models to meet patient communication needs while facilitating sustainable workloads for clinicians.
title: The Role of Measurement in Identifying High-Intensity Secure Message Senders Among Older Adults: Observational Study

summary: The reliability of emergent histopathology foundation models (Histo-FMs) for real-world diagnostic tasks remains unproven. Given the complexity of diagnostic tasks and the challenges inherent in real-world data, we utilized Histo-FMs to investigate their utility for morphological subtyping of Barrett’s esophagus (BE) and detecting esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) across the BE progression spectrum. We benchmarked Histo-FMs on the BarrettNet cohort, spanning diagnostic categories ranging from normal to EAC (N2EAC). The dataset comprised 3528 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs) from 790 patients. A multi-magnification, multi-backbone aggregation of the five most expert-consistent single-scale models yielded incremental performance gains (AUROC of 0.907, F1-score of 0.696, accuracy of 0.795, and κ of 0.651 for morphological subtyping; AUROC of 0.909, F1-score of 0.836, accuracy of 0.959, and κ of 0.673 for EAC detection), with non-uniform gains across single-model comparisons and limited benefit for dysplasia. The findings support the capability of Histo-FMs for BE morphological subtyping and EAC detection in a multicenter clinical cohort, while highlighting persistent challenges in dysplasia assessment and the need for external validation. This study provides a foundation for future clinical validation.
title: Towards reliable morphological subtyping and cancer detection on Barrett’s esophagus pathology through ensembling foundation models
